subtopicTitle: Determinants — cofactor expansion along any row/column

cards.front: Define the minor $M_{ij}$ of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$.
cards.back: The minor $M_{ij}$ of a matrix $A$ is the determinant of the submatrix formed by deleting the $i$-th row and $j$-th column of $A$.

cards.front: Define the cofactor $C_{ij}$ of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$.
cards.back: The cofactor $C_{ij}$ of a matrix $A$ is given by $C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$, where $M_{ij}$ is the minor of $A$ corresponding to the $i$-th row and $j$-th column.

cards.front: State the formula for the determinant of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ using cofactor expansion along the $i$-th row.
cards.back: The determinant of $A$ is given by $\det(A) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}C_{ij} = a_{i1}C_{i1} + a_{i2}C_{i2} + \dots + a_{in}C_{in}$, where $a_{ij}$ are the entries of $A$ and $C_{ij}$ are their corresponding cofactors.

cards.front: State the formula for the determinant of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ using cofactor expansion along the $j$-th column.
cards.back: The determinant of $A$ is given by $\det(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ij}C_{ij} = a_{1j}C_{1j} + a_{2j}C_{2j} + \dots + a_{nj}C_{nj}$, where $a_{ij}$ are the entries of $A$ and $C_{ij}$ are their corresponding cofactors.

cards.front: Calculate $\det(A)$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ using cofactor expansion along the first row.
When using cofactor expansion to find the determinant of a large matrix, which row or column should you choose for expansion to minimize calculations?
cards.back: To minimize calculations, choose the row or column that contains the most zero entries. This is because any term $a_{ij}C_{ij}$ will be zero if $a_{ij}=0$, effectively reducing the number of cofactors that need to be computed.

cards.front: Why does the cofactor expansion method yield the same determinant value regardless of which row or column is chosen for expansion?
cards.back: The determinant is uniquely defined by a set of axioms (multilinearity, alternating property, and $\det(I)=1$). The cofactor expansion is a derived formula that satisfies these axioms. Since the determinant of a matrix is a unique scalar value, any valid method (including cofactor expansion along *any* row or column) must produce this same unique value.
